title: Introduction to Algorithms: Thinking in Steps

questions.question: Which property is NOT required of a valid algorithm?
options: It must run in under one second
It must work for a whole class of inputs
questions.rationale: Algorithms must be finite, unambiguous, effective, and general — but no fixed speed limit is part of the definition.

questions.question: Binary search on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items needs roughly how many comparisons?
questions.rationale: Each comparison halves the range, so about log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 checks suffice.

questions.question: An algorithm with O(n²) time complexity compared to an O(n log n) one will:
options: Grow much slower in running time as n increases
Use no extra memory by definition
questions.rationale: Quadratic growth dominates: for large n, n² vastly exceeds n·log(n), regardless of hardware speed.

questions.question: Merge sort's strategy of splitting the list, sorting halves, and merging them is called:
questions.rationale: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them, and combines results — giving merge sort its O(n log n) average time.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is especially fast when the input is already nearly sorted?
questions.rationale: Insertion sort places each element into the already-sorted prefix and runs near O(n) when few elements are out of place.

questions.question: Accessing an array element by index is an example of which complexity class?
questions.rationale: Per the complexity table, accessing an array element is O(1) — constant time, independent of list size.

questions.question: Trying every subset of a problem's items corresponds to which growth rate?
questions.rationale: The lesson maps 'trying every subset' to O(2ⁿ) — exponential time, the slowest class in the table.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs?
questions.rationale: Bubble sort's idea is swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs repeatedly; it runs in O(n²) average time.

questions.question: In the pseudocode for BINARY-SEARCH, when A[mid] < target, what happens next?
questions.rationale: If the middle value is less than the target, the target must lie in the right half, so low = mid + 1 narrows the search there.

questions.question: According to the definition of correctness, a correct algorithm:
options: Runs in O(log n) or better
Produces the right output for every valid input
Always uses the least possible memory
Never takes more than one pass over the data
questions.rationale: Correctness means producing the right output for every valid input — efficiency (time/memory as input grows) is a separate question.

questions.question: Quicksort partitions data around a pivot and recurses. Its typical average running time is:
questions.rationale: The sorting table lists Quicksort as O(n log n) typical — partition around a pivot, then recurse on both sides.
